title: The Righteous Judge: A Plea of the Falsely Accused
summary: Hunted by pursuers, David takes refuge in the LORD and swears his innocence of the charges against him, calling down disaster on himself if he is guilty. He summons God to take his seat as judge of the nations and to vindicate the righteous. The psalm pictures the wicked falling into the pit they dug for others and ends in thanksgiving to the LORD Most High.
story: The prayers of Book 1 keep returning to the problem of enemies, and Psalm 7 frames it as a court case. David is not only in danger; he has been accused. He appeals to the highest court there is, the LORD who judges the peoples. The psalm develops the promise of Psalm 1 that the way of the wicked will perish, and it shows how that promise works: evil tends to destroy the one who does it. It also widens the lens from David's private trouble to God's rule over all nations, preparing for Psalms 8 and 9, where God's name and throne are praised across the earth.
historical:
The heading calls the psalm a Shiggaion of David, sung to the LORD “concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite”. This Cush is not mentioned anywhere else in the Old Testament, and his identity is unknown. Because Saul came from the tribe of Benjamin, many interpreters place the psalm during the years when Saul's supporters hunted David (1 Samuel 18 to 26), and verse 4 has reminded readers of David's refusal to harm Saul when he had the chance (1 Samuel 24 and 26). Others suggest the time of Absalom's revolt, when the Benjamite Shimei cursed David as a man of blood (2 Samuel 16:5-8). Some have connected Cush with the Cushite messenger of 2 Samuel 18, but that man is not called a Benjamite. None of these identifications can be proved.

As with other headings, scholars differ on whether this one preserves early tradition about the psalm's origin or reflects a later editor's reading of David's life. Either way, the heading invites readers to hear the psalm as the prayer of a man slandered by people close to the royal house.
cultural:
Verses 3 to 5 are an oath of innocence, a legal form known from the ancient Near East and from other parts of the Old Testament (Job 31 is a long example). When evidence was lacking, an accused person could take a solemn oath that called down a curse on himself if he was lying, and so hand the case to God. David does exactly that: if I have done this, let my enemy trample me into the dust.

The courtroom imagery continues. In Israel, the judge sat while the parties stood, and justice was often done at the city gate. Verse 7 pictures the nations gathered around God as he takes his seat on high. Verse 9 says God searches “hearts and minds”, literally hearts and kidneys; in Hebrew thought the kidneys stood for the innermost feelings and motives, much as we speak of the gut. Verses 12 and 13 picture God as a warrior with sword, bow, and flaming arrows, an image familiar from ancient royal art, where kings and gods were shown armed against their enemies. Verse 15 draws on hunting practice: a pit dug and covered to trap an animal.
literary: The heading's word Shiggaion appears only here; a related plural introduces the prayer of Habakkuk 3. Its meaning is uncertain. Some connect it with a verb meaning to wander or reel and think it describes an intense, passionate poem; others link it to a word for lament. The psalm moves in clear stages: a plea for rescue (verses 1 and 2), the oath of innocence (verses 3 to 5), a summons to God as judge (verses 6 to 9), a statement of trust in God's justice (verses 10 to 13), a description of how evil recoils on the evildoer (verses 14 to 16), and a closing vow of praise (verse 17). Verse 14 uses the image of pregnancy in three stages (travails, conceives, births) to show evil growing from intention to act. The final verse introduces the title “LORD Most High”, which Psalm 9 will take up.

outline.t: Heading and plea: save me from my pursuers
Arise, O LORD, and judge the peoples
God the righteous judge, armed against the unrepentant
Evil falls back on its maker
Thanks to the LORD Most High

doctrines.note: God is “a righteous judge”, who sees the heart, vindicates the upright, and opposes evil every day. His judgment is presented as good news for the wronged.
Verse 12 opens a door in the middle of the warning: “If one does not repent”. God's judgment falls on the unrepentant, which means that turning back remains possible.
Verses 15 and 16 describe a moral order in God's world in which violence tends to return on the head of the violent. God often judges by letting evil run its own course to its own ruin.

words.note: Shaphat, to judge. In Hebrew the word covers more than handing down verdicts; it means to govern and to set things right, to rescue the wronged as well as to punish the wrongdoer. That is why the psalmist can ask to be judged (verse 8) and mean it as a request for help.

Tsaddiq, righteous. The word appears three times here and names both God and the people he establishes. In the Psalms the righteous are not the sinless but those who are in the right before God, whose cause is just and who belong to him.

Shuv, to turn or return, here in the sense of repent (verse 12). It is the basic Old Testament word for repentance: turning around on the road and going back toward God. The same verb appears elsewhere in the psalm for evil turning back on the head of the evildoer (verse 16), a play on the word that Hebrew poets enjoyed.

Elyon, Most High. An ancient title for God that stresses his supremacy over every other power; it first appears in Genesis 14, where Melchizedek is priest of God Most High. At the close of this psalm it names the judge to whom the whole case has been appealed.

christ: Jesus, like David, was falsely accused, hunted by those close to power, and refused to take vengeance. Peter says that when he was reviled he did not revile in return but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23), which is the posture of this psalm. The picture of God searching hearts and minds is taken up in Revelation 2:23, where the risen Christ says that he is the one who searches minds and hearts, and the New Testament names Christ as the one through whom God will judge the world (Acts 17:31). The link to Psalm 7 is a pattern of righteous suffering and divine vindication rather than a direct prophecy. There is also a difference: David claims innocence of a particular charge, while Jesus was innocent altogether and bore judgment for others.

hard.q: How can David claim to be righteous and ask God to judge him by his integrity?
hard.a: Read by itself, verse 8 can sound self-righteous, and it seems to clash with texts that say no one is righteous before God (Psalm 143:2). But the psalm is a legal plea about a specific accusation. David is not claiming sinlessness; he is saying that on this charge he is innocent, and he stakes his life on it with an oath. The Old Testament knows the difference between being a sinner in general and being in the right in a particular dispute. Christians have also read such claims more broadly, in light of the righteousness God gives to those who trust him, but the plain sense is courtroom language: vindicate me, because I have not done what they say.

questions: David hands his case to God rather than defending himself by force. When have you been falsely accused, and what would it mean to entrust the verdict to God?
Verse 12 warns that judgment falls on those who do not repent. Where might God be inviting you to turn back before it comes to that?
Verses 15 and 16 say evil often traps the one who plans it. Where have you seen that pattern, in history or in your own life?
